To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
labor-market programs in Sweden do not reduce unemployment, that labor-market programs increase wages, and that labor-market programs reduce employment.

1) the labor-market policy of active labor market programs has not succeeded in lowering unemployment; 2) it has not succeeded in restraining real wages; 3) it may have increased unemployment and reduced employment; 4) it has increased the wage bill; 5) it may have reduced the productivity of the labor force; and 6) it may have led to an increase in the share of the wage bill in the total production costs.
The Swedish unemployment rate is not low by international standards, and that it would be higher still in the absence of labor market programs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of labour market policies on unemployment and wage determination in Sweden during the period 1955–1988.
the effects of labour market policies on unemployment and real wages.
the effects of labour market policy in Sweden, and the effects of the policy changes that took place between 1975 and 1985.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Swedish labor market policy has not been very successful in the sense of reducing unemployment, and that it may even have had a negative effect on employment.
the effects of labor-market programs on unemployment and wage restraint are ambiguous.

the Swedish labour market institutions and labour-market policies have been successful in reducing the unemployment rate, but that this success is not due to the wage restraint induced by the institutions and policies, but to the high level of labour demand.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Swedish labor market is not a model of how to handle unemployment.
we have found that labor-market programs are likely to have strong crowding-in effects on regular employment and that the programs have strong crowing-out effects on wages.
the labor market policies have been successful in reducing the unemployment rate, but that this has not been accomplished without a cost in terms of lower employment and higher real wages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
labor market programs have a significant effect on wages, but not on employment.
the Swedish labor market policies have not been successful.
there are a lot of things to do to help people get jobs, but that the most effective way to reduce unemployment is to raise the wage rate at which firms hire people.
